message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
The study proposes rolling out weekly food waste collection to all 52,000 households from April 2027. It rests on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households and puts the net cost at about £490,000 a year, covered by a provisional £520,000 government allocation.

The pilot is good evidence and is largely well reported. But the study misreads it on flats and inflates participation in the projection. It also overlooks that its main treatment plant can only take about 60% of the projected tonnage. Corrected, the service is no longer clearly within the funding.

## 1. Participation was not "broadly similar" across housing types

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**. Flats participated at a third of the rate of houses. The study (and the author's description) draws the opposite conclusion: that one uniform service can cover the whole district.

The pilot actually shows flats need their own approach, such as communal bins, bin-store locations, liner distribution or targeted communication. That approach will have a cost, which should be included.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%** (2,280 of 4,000 households). Neither housing type's rate was 64%.

The pilot had the same 20% share of flats as the district, so its results can be scaled up by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

That is about **13% less than the 3,290 tonnes** in the study. The pilot also ran from January to June, so summer and the Christmas period are untested. Participation may also drift down once the service is no longer new.

## 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes

Section 4 notes that Brookfield's contracted capacity is 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029, but nothing else in the study reflects this. Even the corrected projection leaves **about 1,070 tonnes a year** with no stated destination. Using the study's own 3,290 tonnes, the gap is about 1,490 tonnes.

The only alternative named is a plant 46 miles away, with no gate fee or haulage cost given. Burning the excess isn't a real option for a statutory separate collection, and it would remove the disposal saving on those tonnes.

## 4. The corrected finances are not clearly covered

The cost arithmetic itself checks out:
- Vehicles: £990,000 over seven years is £141,400 a year.
- Crews: 12 operatives at £34,000 is £408,000.
- Total: £733,400.

The disposal saving depends on the tonnage figures above:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all to Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,000 | Covered, £30k spare |
| Corrected tonnage (2,870 t, all at Brookfield rates) | ~£212,000 | ~£521,000 | Just over |
| Corrected tonnage, saving only on Brookfield's 1,800 t | ~£133,000 | ~£600,000 | **~£80,000 short** |

The real figure depends on what treating the overflow tonnage costs, and the study doesn't give that.

The £520,000 is also **provisional**, yet the vehicles must be ordered in December 2026. That commits £990,000 before the funding is confirmed.

## 5. Costs that are missing

The author says "every cost line is shown." Several appear to be absent:
- **Spare cover:** a reserve vehicle, and cover for crews on leave or off sick. Six crews with no spare is fragile for a weekly statutory service.
- **Supervision and the dedicated phone line and web page** described in Section 6.
- **A separate approach for flats** (see point 1).
- **Treatment of the overflow tonnage** (see point 3).
- **Replacement caddies, and liners after the first three months.** These may be in the £88,000 line, but the study should say so.
- **Financing the £990,000 vehicle purchase.** The study shows depreciation, not the cost of borrowing or the cash outlay.
- **Whether the £34,000 per operative includes on-costs** (employer pension and National Insurance).

## 6. The timetable has no slack

The study plans to:
- order vehicles in December 2026 for March delivery;
- train crews on those vehicles in March;
- deliver caddies to 52,000 households in March;
- start collections on 5 April.

A delay in any of these delays the launch. The study needs a fallback, for example hired vehicles or a phased start. It should also confirm the Council's statutory start date: many English councils had to start weekly food waste collections by 31 March 2026, unless they had transitional arrangements.

## What holds

- **The pilot was well designed.** It used mixed wards, measured weekly, and reported results by housing type. Only that last detail reveals the flats problem.
- **Contamination was low**, under 2% in spot checks at the plant, and missed collections fell after the first month.
- **The pilot arithmetic in Table 1 and the cost arithmetic in Table 2 are correct.**
- **The £74-a-tonne saving** from sending food waste to Brookfield rather than incineration is real for the tonnage Brookfield can take.
- **Satisfaction of 81%** is encouraging. The study should give the survey response rate, since people who use the service are more likely to answer.

## On the author's description

- **"Participation held up across houses and flats."** It didn't: 66% against 21%.
- **"Treatment is local."** That's true only for the first 1,800 tonnes.
- **"Every cost line is shown."** Several are missing (point 5).
- **"Fully covered."** Only on the inflated projection, and only with funding that is still provisional.
- **"Works back from the vehicle lead time."** It does, but with no margin for delay.

## Recommendation

Before Cabinet approves, the study should:
1. Re-project tonnage by housing type using the pilot's actual rates.
2. Set out a plan for flats, with its cost.
3. Secure treatment for the tonnage above 1,800 tonnes, and cost it.
4. Rerun the finances using these figures, and show the gap if the new-burdens funding comes in below £520,000.
5. Add spare vehicle and crew cover, plus a fallback if the vehicles arrive late.

The service is required by law and the pilot shows it can work. As presented, though, the study overstates participation and leaves out the treatment-capacity gap. On corrected figures, it may not be fully funded.
